quote: Kann man einen allgemeinen zwingenden Beweis führen, dass jede Erkenntniss möglich sein muss?
english: Can one give a general compelling proof that every knowledge must be possible?
topic: Philosophical questions on whether human reason can answer every question it poses itself (decidability, squaring the circle, contradictory results), followed by a Plücker-type formula for the dimension of plane algebraic curves.

triage.modern_statement: This is a foundational and philosophical question, not a specific theorem. In modern terms it asks: can one prove that every well-posed (mathematical) question can in principle be decided? That is, is every mathematical problem solvable, which Hilbert called 'no ignorabimus'? In formal terms this becomes: is there a consistent formal system in which every sentence of arithmetic can be either proved or refuted, and is there an algorithm that decides whether any given first-order statement is valid (the Entscheidungsproblem)?
triage.answered_by: Hilbert stated the belief publicly, without proof, as an axiom of solvability in his Paris address of 1900, and repeated it in his 1930 Königsberg address ('Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen'). In the formalized sense the answer was negative. Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) show that every consistent, effectively axiomatized system rich enough for arithmetic contains undecidable sentences. Church and Turing showed independently in 1936 that the Entscheidungsproblem has no algorithmic solution. Later concrete undecidability results include the unsolvability of Hilbert's 10th problem (Matiyasevich and others, 1970), which the arXiv source below also mentions.

evidence.claim: In his 1900 Paris ICM lecture 'Mathematical Problems', Hilbert stated his conviction that every mathematical problem is solvable.
Hilbert put his slogan 'Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen' against du Bois-Reymond's 'ignorabimus', in the 1900 address and again on 8 September 1930.
Church and Turing proved in 1936 that an algorithm deciding the Entscheidungsproblem is impossible.
Turing and Church each reached the negative result that the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable.
The gap between the goals of Hilbert's program and Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem was apparent as soon as Gödel announced his result.
Hilbert believed every mathematical problem has an answer that can be found in finitely many logical steps; this source relates that belief to the unsolvability of Hilbert's 10th problem.

triage.why: The note is an early private form of Hilbert's well-known 'no ignorabimus' thesis. He published it in 1900 in the introduction to the 23 problems, not as one of the problems themselves, and repeated it in 1930. The page context (decidability, squaring the circle as a proof of impossibility) matches this. The question as worded ('every knowledge') is philosophical, but its mathematical core was settled negatively by Gödel (1931) and by Church and Turing (1936). The philosophical side, absolute versus formal undecidability, is still debated. Research on undecidability and independence (logic, computability, set theory) is an active field. Confidence is medium because the note is general and the link to these results is an interpretation, not something Hilbert spells out. The 1931 Gödel and 1970 Matiyasevich details are standard history; the sources found here only mention Gödel's result and Hilbert's 10th problem without those specifics.
